passage: Lata, you want to know how I learned to lose an argument? Sit down, I'm Keerthana and I will tell you. I was twenty, in the college debate group, and I was sure our hostel needed a later gate time. I stood up with my figures, very pleased with myself. Dhruv, at the back, said, "Your survey only asked people on your own floor." My face went hot. I wanted to say that the floor was enough. But he was right, and I knew it, so I said, "You are right about that. Give me a week." I walked through every block with my sheet. The new numbers were messier and the proposal was better. The warden read every page, and Dhruv helped me count the sheets, arguing with me about the results all the way to the canteen.

qa.q: Whose survey only asked people on one floor, and who pointed this out?
qa.a: Keerthana's survey only asked people on Keerthana's own floor, and Dhruv pointed it out from the back of the debate group.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling when Dhruv spoke, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Keerthana felt stung and embarrassed. Their face went hot and they wanted to say the floor was enough, before choosing to admit the point.

qa.q: What did Keerthana decide to do after Dhruv's remark, and how did it change the proposal?
qa.a: Keerthana admitted Dhruv was right, asked for a week and went to every block. The numbers were messier but the proposal was better and the warden read every page.

qa.q: How might Dhruv have felt when Keerthana said "You are right about that"?
qa.a: Dhruv probably felt heard and respected, since Keerthana did not defend the weak survey and later even counted sheets together with Dhruv. 🙂

grounding: A young adult concedes a good counter-argument, adjusts the plan and gains credibility, told by the elder as a memory.

passage:
Twelve minutes before their final viva, Samir and Vandana were still arguing over the slide order in the corridor outside the seminar room.
"Numbers first," Samir said. "The examiners like proof."
"If they do not care about the problem, the numbers are just noise," Vandana said, holding the laptop against a hip. "Open with the woman from the survey who walked four kilometres for water."
Samir looked at the clock, then at the slides. His jaw tightened and loosened. "Fair point. Story first. But the biggest number goes in your opening sentence."
"Deal."
They dragged three slides, fixed one title, and walked in with the projector already warm.

qa.q: How many minutes were left before the viva when the argument began?
qa.a: Twelve minutes were left before their final viva.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling when the jaw tightened and then loosened?
qa.a: Samir felt pressured and a little reluctant, since the clock was running and the plan was theirs. Then Samir let go of the argument and accepted the better order.

qa.q: What did Samir change after saying "Fair point", and what stayed the same?
qa.a: Samir agreed to put the story first, and kept the proof by asking that the biggest number go in Vandana's opening sentence.

qa.q: What would it have been like for Vandana if Samir had kept insisting on numbers first?
qa.a: Vandana would probably have felt unheard and anxious, with the clock running and the argument still going as they walked in. Samir's quick concession left them free to prepare.

grounding: Under time pressure, a young adult says a fair point was made and changes the slide order to suit the better argument.
